prize_parts.citation: For the development of general, ligand-controlled palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange my preferred configuration is unchanged: B052 as the whole prize, credited to Buchwald and Hartwig. It is the one position that four members place in their preferred configuration and that three more list as an alternative, but I rest the case on the chemistry. The advance was ligand design guided by mechanism: control of oxidative addition, amide binding and reductive elimination turned a narrow, harsh reaction into a general one, and three decades of use in pharmaceutical, agrochemical and materials synthesis show the consequences. That meets my test of a game-changer that is simple in concept and already proven. The round-1 files also removed my main worry about the credit. Every B052 supporter names exactly the same two people, nobody argues for three, and Zou and Somfai give a clear reason why Kosugi's stoichiometric tin-amide reaction was a precursor and not the general, ligand-controlled method. I have tightened the citation to say 'general, ligand-controlled' so that it describes what Buchwald and Hartwig did and does not overclaim for the whole C-N field.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection stands: the committee honoured Pd cross-coupling in 2010, and Linke and Sparr are right that this adds a new bond type and a better catalyst class, not a new organising concept. I think the ligand and mechanistic work is real chemistry and not a substrate-scope extension, but I cannot show that to a colleague who weighs conceptual novelty above demonstrated consequence. Kosugi's priority still cannot be settled from the files before us, and Brzezinski, Sparr and Somfai all want the expert report to confirm it. Hartwig's presence on the C-H functionalisation entry means the citation must stay confined to C-N coupling. Finally, a single-part prize leaves out the biomedical achievements that several members value, base editing in particular.

responses.point: Heiner holds B002 first for conceptual novelty, accepts B052 as the more defensible choice if attribution and demonstrated consequence outweigh novelty, and says condensate relevance and the Rosen, Pappu and Mittag credit remain open.
responses.response: I take your point that condensates introduce a new organising idea and that B052 extends a logic the committee already honoured. My criterion differs: a prize should reward what has already changed practice, and here the weak point is not the in vitro thermodynamics but how far the in-cell claims hold. Chabes, Brzezinski and Sparr independently raise the same worry about overexpression and imaging, and you list it first among your own uncertainties. Brzezinski also shows that Hyman and Brangwynne alone omit the multivalency work, while adding Rosen still leaves Pappu and Mittag out. A citation resting on the 2009 P-granule result and a three-name cap therefore risks crediting the phenomenon and not the chemistry. I would reopen B002 if the expert report separates the established principle from the contested cellular claims, but I do not move it above B052 today.

responses.point: Daniel proposes a two-part prize, B052 for Buchwald and Hartwig plus B004 for Liu alone, as a balance of a mature method and a newer biomolecular tool, using the three-name limit as two plus one.
responses.response: I considered this seriously, since it was the only second part I would entertain. I still decline it, for three reasons. Your own case_against concedes that Liu alone leaves out Komor and Gaudelli, and Chabes says he would resist dropping either, so the Liu-alone credit is not a settled answer. Kondo and Nishida's Target-AID is an independent line, and the three-name limit then forces an exclusion for which I see no evidence in the files. Last, Aili, Chabes and Brzezinski agree that clinical safety data are still emerging and that the 2020 CRISPR prize is close. Adding B004 now would bind a mature, cleanly credited prize to a part whose credit we have not resolved. If the committee prefers two parts I would accept it as a second ballot choice, but not as my preferred configuration.

responses.point: Andrei argues that base editing is new chemistry because the adenine editor needed directed evolution of a deaminase with no natural DNA substrate, that replication is solid, and that Liu, Komor and Gaudelli can be credited under citation wording that names the invention and not one editor.
responses.response: That is the best case for B004 I have seen, and I accept that the adenine deaminase evolution makes it more than re-targeting Cas9; it is why B004 stays my first alternative. My remaining difficulty is precedent and attribution, not chemistry. Crediting Komor and Gaudelli alongside Liu is defensible, but then Nishida and Kondo's near-simultaneous Target-AID has to be explained in terms of who conceived each editor class, and Liu's name also sits on prime editing. Your suggestion to let the citation name base editing and not an editor is sensible. I would still want the expert report to settle that credit before a final ballot, and I do not accept that it is as ready as B052.

responses.point: Peter backs B009 for Gray and Winkler as a mechanism-first, cleanly credited discovery, but accepts that B052 is the strongest case on impact and maturity and wants the report to confirm priority over Kosugi.
responses.response: We agree that a mechanism that explains a process outweighs a bare method, and as a theoretician I find electron-transfer theory attractive. For that reason I would add the mechanistic work in B052, which is the part that makes it a discovery, to my case. I would not support B009 as a prize, though, for the reasons you give: the Marcus theory overlap, and Hopfield and Dutton and Moser outside the credited pair. On Kosugi I agree that the report should settle the 1994-1995 record, and since nobody asks to credit him, I think a citation worded around the general, ligand-controlled method is sufficient and avoids the priority question without an arbitrary third name.

uncertainties: Kosugi's and Migita-type precursors: whether the 1994-1995 record shows tin-amide coupling as general enough to share the discovery, which I cannot verify from the files.
Whether the committee will treat B052 as too close to the 2010 cross-coupling prize, and whether Linke, Sparr and Chabes hold that against it.
Whether B004 attribution (Liu, Komor, Gaudelli versus Kondo and Nishida) can be resolved, and whether a two-part prize pairing it with B052 would then be better than my single part.
Whether the in vivo evidence for condensates will narrow enough to move B002 up, and how Pappu and Mittag would be handled under the three-name cap.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal is needed. My Warshel/EVB, ribosome and Uppsala connections do not touch B052, B004, B037 or B002, and none of the credited people is a collaborator, student or colleague. Nothing in the round-1 exchange changes this disclosure.
